subtitle: Decide what a navigator role is for, write a clear scope, choose where the role lives and how it is paid, and supervise it so the work lasts, without quietly adding it to bilingual staff members' jobs.
audience: For supervisors, managers, program leads and HR partners considering navigator or broker roles. It is a planning guide, not a classification, bargaining or budget decision; those stay with Minnesota Management and Budget, agency HR and the responsible managers.

lessons.title: Start with what the role is for
objectives: Tie a navigator role to specific decision points where people are being lost or misunderstood.
Decide which communities and which processes the role will serve first.
Name the outcomes you hope to change before the role is created.
Explain why a role for "everyone, everywhere" is likely to fail.
lessons.teaching:
Navigator roles work best when they have a clear job to do. The strongest evidence comes from navigation tied to a specific step. In a 2021 randomized trial, family navigation for young children who screened positive for autism raised the share who got a diagnostic answer within a year, and the gap was largest for Hispanic families. The authors also found that results varied by site. A navigator attached to a clear decision point has something specific to change.

So before writing a position, find where people are getting lost. Look at your own process. Where do referrals go cold? Where do assessments get rescheduled again and again? Where do renewals lapse? Which communities show up less in services than in the population you serve? The answers point to where a navigator could help first.

Then choose. A single navigator cannot serve every community and every process. Decide which communities the role will serve, which languages it needs and which steps it will focus on. Involve the communities themselves. Researchers studying a Virginia family support program recommend that providers work closely with families to decide brokers' roles and how support is offered.

Finally, name what you hope will change, before the role exists. Fewer missed assessments? Shorter time from referral to services? More people choosing culturally responsive providers? A clear purpose makes the role easier to explain, easier to supervise and easier to defend when budgets get tight.
lessons.keyPoint: Tie the role to the steps where people are being lost, choose who and what it serves first and name what should change.
lessons.example: Practice case: The program manager has funding for one navigator position. A senior leader suggests the navigator should "help any family who needs it, in any language, at any step."
lessons.question: What should the program manager propose?
choices: Use the program's own data and community input to pick one or two steps and communities to focus on first, with outcomes to watch.
Accept the broad role, since flexibility will help the most families.
Delay the position until there is funding for a navigator in every language.
feedback: This gives the role a clear purpose, grounds it in where people are actually being lost and makes success visible.
Broad roles sound helpful but spread one person too thin, and it becomes hard to show what changed.
Waiting for complete coverage may mean no navigation at all. A focused start can grow.
lessons.reflection: In your program, where do you think people are most often lost or misunderstood? What would you look at to check?
lessons.action: Pick one step in your process and find out how often people drop out or get stuck there. Note which communities are affected most.

check.question: What does the evidence suggest about where navigation helps most?
check.correct: Where it is tied to a specific step or decision point, though results can vary by setting.
wrong: Where one navigator covers every service and community.
Only in health care, never in social services.
check.feedback: The strongest results, such as the 2021 autism family navigation trial, come from navigation attached to a specific step. The same trial found results varied by site, so a focused role still needs watching.

lessons.title: Write the scope
objectives: List the duties a navigator role will carry, using recognized descriptions of the work.
Name clearly what the role is not.
Describe qualifications that value community knowledge and lived experience.
Connect the scope to the state's position description process.
lessons.teaching:
A written scope protects the navigator, the people they serve and the staff they work with. Start with the duties. The C3 Project, a national effort to describe community health worker roles, lists ten roles, including cultural mediation among individuals, communities and health and social service systems; care coordination, case management and system navigation; advocating for individuals and communities; conducting outreach; and participating in evaluation and research. Not every navigator does all of these, but the list helps you choose deliberately.

Next, write what the role is not. A navigator is not an interpreter unless they are qualified and hired to interpret. A navigator does not decide eligibility or services. A navigator does not carry a case manager's caseload. A navigator is not the agency's messenger for bad news or enforcement. Saying this in writing makes it easier for everyone to hold the line when a busy week tempts them to blur it.

Qualifications should value what makes navigators effective. Community knowledge, trust and lived experience can matter as much as a degree. Language skills may be essential for some roles. Knowledge of the system can often be taught; trust in a community usually cannot.

In Minnesota state government, positions are described in a position description, which Minnesota Management and Budget explains is used mainly for classification and filling vacancies. Work with your HR partner early, so the duties you write are reflected in how the role is classified and paid. The course Cultural Broker as a Role goes deeper on writing a scope you can hold.
lessons.keyPoint: Write the duties, write what the role is not and value community knowledge. Work with HR so the position description matches the real job.
lessons.example: Practice case: The supervisor drafts a navigator scope. It includes outreach and helping families through assessments, but also "interpreting as needed" and "carrying overflow cases when the team is short."
lessons.question: What should the program manager suggest?
choices: Keep it as written. Flexibility will help the team.
Remove interpreting unless the person is qualified and hired for it, remove the overflow caseload and add a short "what this role is not" section.
Remove outreach, since it is hard to measure.
feedback: Flexibility like this turns the navigator into an interpreter and a case manager, and the navigation work disappears.
This keeps the role focused on navigation and gives everyone a written line to hold when a busy week tempts them to blur it.
Outreach is often the heart of navigation, and it can be measured, for example by how many people complete the next step.
lessons.reflection: In your team, which roles have quietly grown to include work that was never in the description? What did that cost?
lessons.action: Draft a five-line "what this role is not" list for a navigator position, or for a role you already supervise.

check.question: Which belongs in a navigator scope's "what this role is not" section?
check.correct: Deciding eligibility or services, and interpreting unless qualified and hired to do it.
wrong: Helping families understand the steps of a process.
Telling the agency where a process keeps breaking down.
check.feedback: Explaining the process and feeding back problems are core navigation work. Decisions belong to staff, and interpretation is a separate, qualified role.

lessons.title: Where the role lives and how it is paid
objectives: Compare a navigator position inside the agency with navigation through a community partner.
Identify possible ways a role could be funded, and check them with the people who decide.
Recognize and stop unpaid navigation work by bilingual or bicultural staff.
Plan for the role to last beyond one budget cycle or one person.
lessons.teaching:
A navigator can sit inside the agency or work through a community partner, and each has strengths. An internal position may have easier access to systems and colleagues. A partner organization may have deeper trust in the community, and the navigator may be seen as being on the family's side rather than the agency's. M Health Fairview's cultural brokers, for example, are part of the health system but spend most of their time based at trusted community organizations.

Funding shapes what is possible. Some navigation is already paid for elsewhere. MNsure-certified navigators offer free help with health coverage. In health care, the Minnesota Department of Health notes that Minnesota Health Care Programs cover some community health worker services, including Community Health Integration services that include system navigation. Whether any of this fits your program is a question for your budget office and program leaders, not an assumption to build on.

The most common unfunded navigation is invisible. A bilingual or bicultural staff member gets asked to "just come along," explain a letter or call a family, on top of their own job. It feels like teamwork, but it is unpaid work that nobody counts, and it can leave that person caught between their community and their job. If this is happening on your team, name it, count it and either make it part of a defined, recognized role or move the work to one.

Plan for the role to last. Write down how referrals reach the navigator, who supervises them and how the work will be funded next year. A role that depends on one person's goodwill, or one year's money, often disappears just as communities start to trust it.
lessons.keyPoint: Choose where the role lives on purpose, check funding with the people who decide and stop asking bilingual staff to navigate for free.
lessons.example: Practice case: The budget for a navigator position is cut. A manager suggests the team "rely on our bilingual staff for now," asking them to help families on top of their caseloads.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor do?
choices: Agree. The families need help and the staff are willing.
Tell bilingual staff they may not help families in their language under any circumstances.

Explain that this would be unpaid, uncounted work, and propose options: a partnership with a community organization, recognizing the work in those staff members' roles or a smaller, funded navigation role.
feedback: Willingness is not a plan. This quietly adds a second job to a few people and hides the real cost.
This avoids extraction, but it also stops ordinary, appropriate help. The problem is unrecognized extra work, not the language skill.
This names the problem and offers paths that treat navigation as real work, so the families get help and the staff are treated fairly.
lessons.reflection: Who on your team is most often asked to help with work outside their role because of their language or background? Has anyone ever counted it?
lessons.action: For one month, keep a simple count of navigation-type requests made to staff outside their roles. Bring the count to your next planning conversation.

check.question: Why is asking bilingual staff to navigate on top of their jobs a problem?
check.correct: It is unpaid, uncounted work that can leave them caught between their community and their job, and it hides the real need.
wrong: Because bilingual staff should never use their language skills at work.
Because navigation is not real work.
check.feedback: Language skills are valuable at work. The problem is adding navigation to someone's job without recognizing, planning or paying for it.

lessons.title: Supervising and supporting the role
objectives: Provide supervision that understands both the system and the community side of the work.
Protect the navigator's trust in the community by keeping them out of enforcement and bad-news roles.
Watch for secondary traumatic stress and set caseloads and supports to reduce it.
Review the role with navigators and communities as it grows.
lessons.teaching:
Navigators carry two sets of expectations: the agency's and the community's. Good supervision understands both. Meet regularly, ask what the navigator is seeing and help them solve problems in the system. A supervisor who only counts contacts will miss what makes the role valuable.

Protect the navigator's trust. When a navigator is used to deliver bad news, enforce a rule or check up on a family, the community may start to see them as part of the problem. If a family needs to hear a hard decision, the staff member responsible should deliver it. The navigator can be there to help the family understand it and know their options, if the family wants that.

Navigators hear hard stories, often from people in their own community. The National Child Traumatic Stress Network describes secondary traumatic stress as emotional distress that results from hearing about another person's firsthand trauma. Its fact sheet names risk factors that fit this work, such as heavy caseloads, isolation and unresolved personal trauma. It also names supports that help, such as supervision, balanced caseloads, flexible scheduling and ongoing training. The micro course Sustaining the Navigator goes further.

Review the role as it grows. Ask navigators and the communities they serve what is working and what is not, and adjust the scope. A role designed with the people it serves is more likely to earn their trust and to last.
lessons.keyPoint: Supervise both sides of the work, keep navigators out of enforcement and bad-news roles, and plan caseloads and support for the weight they carry.
lessons.example: Practice case: A family's services are being reduced. The supervisor's manager suggests that the navigator, who knows the family well, should be the one to tell them.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor do?
choices: Have the responsible staff member deliver the decision and explain how to ask for a review, and offer the family the navigator's help understanding it if they want it.
Ask the navigator to tell the family, since the family trusts them.
Keep the navigator away from the family until the decision is final.
feedback: This keeps the decision with the person responsible for it, gives the family their options and lets the navigator support them rather than deliver the news.
This spends the navigator's trust on a decision they did not make, and it can change how the community sees them.
Cutting the family off from their navigator at a hard moment can leave them alone just when they need help most.
lessons.reflection: What would help a navigator on your team feel supported, rather than only managed?
lessons.action: Add two questions to your regular check-in with any navigator or community-facing staff member: What are you seeing that we should fix? What is weighing on you?

check.question: Which practice best protects a navigator's trust with the community?
check.correct: Having the responsible staff deliver decisions and enforcement, with the navigator offering support if the family wants it.
wrong: Having the navigator deliver hard news, since the family trusts them.
Having the navigator monitor families for compliance.
check.feedback: When navigators carry the agency's hard messages or enforcement, communities can start to see them as part of the system they help people through. Keep those tasks with the responsible staff.

cards.back: Tie the role to the steps where people are lost, and name what should change.
A national list of ten community health worker roles, including cultural mediation, system navigation, advocacy and outreach.
Not an interpreter unless qualified, not a decision-maker, not a case manager and not the agency's messenger for bad news.
Bilingual or bicultural staff asked to navigate on top of their jobs. Name it, count it and make it a recognized role.
Keep navigators out of enforcement and bad-news roles.
Distress from hearing about others' trauma. Supervision, balanced caseloads and training help.

Write what the role is not.

Work with HR on the position description early.
